briefing.text: Tumour purity can confound bulk-expression signature scores such as HYPOXIA_SCORE, because stromal and immune content shift the score and TP53-mutant tumours often differ in purity. Correlate TUMOR_PURITY with HYPOXIA_SCORE and compare purity by TP53_STATUS. If purity is related to either, fit HYPOXIA_SCORE ~ TP53_STATUS + TUMOR_PURITY (plus other relevant covariates) and judge the hypothesis on the adjusted TP53 coefficient. Check whether adjustment changes its size or sign.
briefing.reason: A raw TP53 difference may only reflect purity. This adjustment can reverse the direction of the effect and so change the label.

briefing.text: The expression PROCESSING_BATCH can shift HYPOXIA_SCORE. If batches are unbalanced by TP53 status, a batch effect can look like a TP53 effect, or hide one (Simpson's paradox). Cross-tab PROCESSING_BATCH by TP53_STATUS and compare HYPOXIA_SCORE across batches. If either is unbalanced, include batch as a fixed effect or compare within batch rather than using pooled raw means. If batch and TP53 status are almost completely confounded, say that the effect cannot be separated from batch.
briefing.reason: Batch imbalance can create, hide or flip the pooled TP53 difference.

briefing.text: SITE (hospital) can confound the comparison if sites differ in TP53 mutation prevalence and in sample handling. Ischaemia time strongly induces hypoxia genes. Cross-tab SITE by TP53_STATUS and HYPOXIA_SCORE by SITE. If needed, adjust for site or stratify by it.
briefing.reason: Site differences in pre-analytical handling directly affect hypoxia scores and could explain a TP53 difference.

briefing.text: data_clinical_sample.txt may hold several samples per patient (primary and metastasis), while TP53 status may be recorded per patient. Sample type can also shift hypoxia scores. Count samples per PATIENT_ID and cross-tab SAMPLE_TYPE by TP53_STATUS. Do not treat samples as independent. Analyse one row per patient (primary tumour preferred, or the per-patient mean), or use a mixed model with a patient random effect. Adjust for or stratify by sample type, and report the primary-only comparison as the main result.
briefing.reason: Pseudoreplication inflates n and gives undue weight to some patients. If metastases are unevenly spread across TP53 groups, they confound the raw comparison.

briefing.text: TP53 status may be misclassified. TP53_STATUS can disagree with TP53_VAF (status 1 with VAF 0, or the reverse) or be missing. Very low VAF values (under about 0.05-0.10) may be subclonal or artefacts. Tabulate TP53_STATUS against TP53_VAF and count inconsistent, missing and low-VAF cases. Run a sensitivity analysis that excludes these cases and report whether the conclusion holds. Do not use VAF as a dose variable, because VAF depends on purity.
briefing.reason: Misclassifying the exposure can weaken or distort the group comparison, so the conclusion needs to be shown to be robust.

briefing.text: The hypothesis is directional: mutants have higher scores. Before testing, inspect HYPOXIA_SCORE for missing values, sentinel codes (such as -999 or 0), outliers and skew, and recode sentinels as missing. Use a rank-based test (Wilcoxon) together with adjusted linear regression, and report the direction, effect size and CI of the adjusted TP53 effect. A two-sided non-significant result is not by itself evidence against the hypothesis. A clear difference in the opposite direction, or a precise null, is.
briefing.reason: Sentinel values can drive a t-test, and mapping the result onto True/False depends on direction and precision, not only on a p-value.

briefing.text: Merging the patient and sample tables on PATIENT_ID can silently drop or duplicate rows, for example through ID format or whitespace mismatches or duplicate patient rows. Compare row counts before and after the merge, check that IDs are unique in the patient table, and count unmatched IDs. Fix ID formats and remove duplicates before analysis.
briefing.reason: Silent row loss or duplication changes group sizes and can bias the comparison.

shared_assumptions: Both treat processing batch as a nuisance to adjust for; neither asked whether batch could lie on a path between TP53 status and hypoxia (e.g. assay run order linked to tumour type or sample age).
Both assume a linear additive model (TP53 + batch + purity + site) with a constant TP53 effect across sample types; no interaction of TP53 with sample type was reported.
Both assume 'tumour' in the hypothesis covers primaries and metastases alike; Team A chose primary-only as main analysis, Team B pooled all samples.
unused_evidence: data_clinical_supplement.txt (ECOG_PS, BMI, FOLLOW_UP_MONTHS) was not used by either team; ECOG/BMI could mark disease severity linked to both TP53 status and tumour hypoxia.

IFNG_SIGNATURE_SCORE from the same expression assay was not used; it could serve as a negative-control signature to test whether the TP53 difference is a general assay/scale shift rather than hypoxia-specific.
TP53_VAF as a continuous variable (dose-response within mutants) was used only as a low-VAF exclusion by Team A and not at all by Team B.
Patient serum labs (calcium, cholesterol, creatinine) were not examined; likely irrelevant, but unchecked.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A named unmeasured handling effects (e.g. ischaemia time) as weakest point and only reported it; no negative-control check (e.g. IFNG signature) was run to bound it.
Team B's weakest point (self-directed audit, no pitfalls passed down) was stated but not addressed by any additional structured check; Team B's pitfalls_checked list is empty.
second_readings: 'Patients' with TP53-mutant tumours could mean a per-patient comparison of primary tumours only versus all tumour samples including metastases; the agreed direction should be shown to hold in both, including metastasis-only.
'Higher hypoxia score' could be read as a raw score difference or one after removing batch effects; both teams report both, so this reading is likely resolved.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed answer fairly well: the TP53 coding agrees fully with VAF (180 mutant all VAF>0, 150 wild-type all VAF=0), there is one sample per patient, and both teams found the effect in every batch. The checks still open are the unused supplement covariates, a negative-control signature, and whether the effect holds in metastases; none of these looks likely to reverse it.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You did not use data_clinical_supplement.txt. Please merge it and check whether ECOG_PS or BMI differ by TP53 status and relate to HYPOXIA_SCORE, and whether adding them to your adjusted model changes the TP53 coefficient's sign or size. Does this change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your weakest point is unmeasured handling effects. Please run the same adjusted comparison on IFNG_SIGNATURE_SCORE as a negative-control signature from the same assay, and report whether TP53 status shifts it similarly. Does the result change your confidence that the difference is hypoxia-specific?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your main analysis is primary-only. Please report the TP53 comparison in metastases alone and test a TP53 x sample-type interaction. Does the effect hold in metastases, and does this change how you state the conclusion for 'patients with TP53-mutant tumours'?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your pooled analysis mixes 81 metastases with primaries. Please report the TP53 comparison separately within primaries and within metastases and test a TP53 x sample-type interaction. Does this change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You did not use data_clinical_supplement.txt. Please merge it and check whether ECOG_PS or BMI are associated with both TP53 status and HYPOXIA_SCORE, and whether adjusting for them changes the TP53 coefficient. Does this change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Please run the same batch-adjusted comparison on IFNG_SIGNATURE_SCORE as a negative control, and check within mutants whether HYPOXIA_SCORE rises with TP53_VAF. Do these results change your confidence that the difference reflects TP53 status rather than an assay artefact?

When comparing a gene-expression signature score between two genotype groups in bulk tumour data, what is the accepted practice for using a second, unrelated signature from the same assay as a negative control for technical or pre-analytical artefacts?
questions.why: Neither team ran a check for assay-wide shifts. A negative control would show whether the group difference is specific to hypoxia.

findings.question: When comparing a gene-expression signature score between two genotype groups in bulk tumour data, what is the accepted practice for using a second, unrelated signature from the same assay as a negative control for technical or pre-analytical artefacts?
findings.answer: The web did not settle this: all 3 research calls failed with HTTP 403, so no page was read. From general knowledge, unverified: treat it as a negative-control outcome (Lipsitch et al. 2010). Score a signature from the same assay that should not depend on TP53 and run the same comparison and model (same covariates, e.g. batch, site, purity, sample type). If the control differs between groups by a similar standardized effect, the hypoxia difference is likely an assay-wide technical or pre-analytical artefact. If the control is null while hypoxia differs, that supports specificity but does not prove it. Ischaemia/handling time selectively induces hypoxia genes, so you still need to adjust for site/batch. Random-signature work (Venet et al. 2011) shows that unrelated signatures often show associations, which is the reason specificity checks are needed.
